title: God's Judgment and Restoration
english: The people were stubborn and disobedient, leading a life that was detestable and utterly contrary to the law.
God, who manages all things, had allowed them to suffer a blow and be scourged by their enemies, and had given them a taste of the most pleasant things, but they had not responded.

Now, God makes a proclamation, promising that He will bring back those who have already been taken captive and will free them from the bonds of their affliction, and will deliver those who previously conquered into the hands of enemies.

It was likely that, even if they had remained unmoved by those things, they would now choose to be envied by others, and would be lifted up into hope of the things they desired, and would honor the most beloved service to God, and keep their mind unwavering towards Him.

Many had invaded the land of the Jews at various times, but the Chaldeans, who were more savage and wild, and those who ruled Babylon, were the first to be spoken to by the word of prophecy, which says, 'Raise a sign on a bare mountain' (Isaiah 13:2).

Cyrus, the son of Cambyses and the father of Mandane, who ruled over the Persians and Medes, made war against Babylon and the whole land of the Chaldeans, which was large and very extensive, and he prevailed.
It seems that the interpretation of these events is necessary to understand the choices that were made, and to have made a choice of the most necessary things.
The Chaldean nation was not conquered by human strength or military might, for it was unconquerable and unopposed due to its multitude and well-trained tactics.

However, God allowed the conqueror to overcome those who opposed him and to subdue the impiety of the Babylonians, for the most part, sorcery was prevalent among them, and the number of idols was greater.

In fact, the land was even named after these idols, either due to their multitude or because each of the inhabitants had given themselves over to idolatry without restraint, succumbing to error without control.
Furthermore, the Babylonians had desecrated the holy land of Judaea, burning Jerusalem and the divine temple, and taking the sacred vessels to their own land.
In their uncontrolled anger, they slaughtered the Israelites, a holy people and a portion of God's inheritance.
This was not a surprise to those familiar with the sacred scriptures, for it is clear that God handed over the idolatrous Israel to the hands of their enemies, and they were not punished lightly.

title: Deserted Places
english: The desolate state of the land is a result of its complete abandonment, for it is known that the nations of the Saracens, as well as the Assyrians, and even the innermost desert, are referred to as Arabs, given their proximity to the Arabs.
It is likely that the Saracens from Arabia also roam around the deserts of the Assyrians.
Wild beasts will rest there, and the houses will be filled with sound (Isaiah 13:21-22).
This means that the houses will have no inhabitants, and instead, they will be filled with the sounds of desolation.
Demons are said to haunt desolate places, making them their dwelling, and it is there that they will dance.
Sirens, which are birds known for their beautiful singing, or possibly owls, according to the Hebrew translation, will also rest in these deserted areas.
The wild donkeys are referred to as centaurs, and hedgehogs with sharp thorns are likened to frightened mice.
All these creatures are naturally drawn to deserted cities or houses.
The descents into these areas are automatic and planned, almost as if they were discovered by the very fact of what has happened.
In the deserts and silent places, a faint echo can be heard, which seems to emanate from the great silence, and this sound is disturbing, entering the ears of those who are resting.
As a result, wild beasts will rest in these areas, and the houses will be filled with sound, having no human inhabitants.
Demons will dance there, as they are known to haunt desolate places and make them their dwelling.
The presence of centaurs and hedgehogs with sharp thorns, which are like frightened mice, is also characteristic of these deserted areas.
All these elements are fitting for deserted cities or houses, and it is said that this state will come quickly, without delay.

This desolation may bring bitter worry to the Assyrians or a notable calling to the Israelites, for when they were in captivity, they thought they would be freed when the Persians and Medes, along with the Babylonians, campaigned.
In this context, a promise is made to the Israelites that they will experience a swift release from their troubles, and that their prayers will not be delayed, but will be answered quickly.
The Lord will have mercy on Jacob and choose Israel again, and they will rest on their land, with strangers being added to them.
Nations will take them and bring them to their place, and they will inherit and multiply on the land of God, serving as slaves and slave women.
Those who took them captive will be captives, and those who ruled over them will be ruled over, and this will occur on that day.

title: Divine Judgment on Babylon as Instrument of Wrath
english: The Lord has despised his people Jacob, scattering the inheritance of his Israel.
Therefore it is utterly monstrous to trample upon the land of the Lord — that is, the Church — and to fulfill the acts of bloodshed against the people allotted to Christ.
No one who consorts with such foreign crimes can ever be pure.
One might suppose that the speaker has in mind the calamities that have befallen Judea and Jerusalem themselves.

Or perhaps the Babylonian tyrant came as a deserter, laid waste the land of the Judeans, and took the holy city — not because God permitted it, but because he did not give it to him; yet the prophet Isaiah says to us: 'The Lord shall hiss for the fly at the end of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee in the land of the Assyrians, and they shall come and rest in the valleys of the land, and in the clefts of the rocks, and into the caves, and into every fissure, and in every tree.'
How then, by serving the inclinations of such a one, does the Babylonian hold inexpiable guilt, and thus be punished so terribly that beyond nothing remains visible of the wrath brought upon him?
Yes, and very reasonably so.
For God most high indeed wished to turn away the apostate Israel, to examine him with measured chastisements, and to persuade him to return to his accustomed worship — that is, the legal worship.
But he, though inclined to this, proved unyielding like a beast, made use of inflexible angers, and indeed accuses God of speaking plainly.

I have burned with zeal for Jerusalem and for Zion, and my wrath grows hot against the nations that have allied themselves against her. Though my anger was but a spark, they have fanned it into a flame, joining together to do evil.

Just as Pharaoh, already ripe for punishment, was stirred up by his own stumblings—a vessel full of wrath and fury—so that he might display his power and the exact justice of God, so too shall you consider the Babylonians.

For they are instruments of wrath, justly deserving punishment, and were sent against Jerusalem to chastise Israel; after that, they too may seek the punishment most fitting and harmonious for their own deeds.
O wicked offspring, prepare your children to be slaughtered for the sins of your father, lest they rise up and fill the earth with war.
And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will blot out their name, their remnant, and their offspring.

Nabuchodonosor has wrought terrible things against every nation, and those who came after him, even those born of him down to Baltasar, following their father’s evils, have surpassed him in savagery and cruelty.
